parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 12. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a woman who works at a recruitment agency phoning a man who is looking for a job. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5. Sam: Hello? Rachel: Oh, hello. Is that Sam Ellis? Sam: Speaking. Rachel: Hi Sam, this is Rachel Moore from Westbury Recruitment. You came into our office a couple of weeks ago and registered for part-time work. Sam: Oh yes, hello. Thanks for calling. Rachel: Well, a job has just come in that I think might suit you. You mentioned that you'd like to work outdoors, or at least not be sitting in an office all day. Sam: That's right. I did office work for nearly fifteen years, and I'd really like a change. Rachel: Well, this is a position for a sales assistant, and it's at a garden centre just outside town. Sam: Oh, that sounds nice. Which one is it? There are a couple around here. Rachel: It's called Hollins Garden Centre. It's the big one with the glasshouses. Sam: Hollins. I think I've driven past it. Is it on the main road to Oxley? Rachel: No, I think that's a different one. Hollins is on Harcombe Lane. Sam: Sorry, could you spell that for me? Rachel: Sure. It's H, A, R, C, O, M, B, E. Harcombe Lane. Sam: Got it, thanks. Rachel: The full address is on the job description, which I'll email to you later. Sam: Great. So what would I be doing? Mainly working on the tills? Rachel: Well, you'd spend some time on the tills, of course, but the manager told me that the main part of the job is giving customers advice, you know, about which plants would suit their gardens and how to look after them, that kind of thing. Sam: Right. Well, I've got quite a big garden myself, so I know a bit about plants. Rachel: That's good. You'd also be watering and arranging the plants on display, and they want someone who's willing to help out in the restaurant when it gets busy, which is mostly at weekends. Sam: That's fine. I don't mind that at all. Rachel: And finally, you'd be checking deliveries when they arrive, making sure that everything that was ordered has actually come. Sam: OK. That all sounds quite varied. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10. Rachel: Now, there are a few requirements. The most important one is that you must have a driving licence, because sometimes you'd need to take the van out to deliver larger items to customers' homes. Sam: No problem. I've had a licence for over twenty years. Rachel: Good. They also say that experience of working in a shop would be useful, but it isn't essential. They're happy to train the right person. Sam: That's a relief, because I've never actually worked in a shop. Rachel: Another thing they mention is that the job can be quite demanding. You'd be on your feet all day, lifting bags of compost and moving heavy pots around, so they need someone who is physically fit. Sam: Well, I go running three times a week, so I should be fine. Rachel: And of course they'd like someone with a real interest in gardening, which clearly you have. Sam: Definitely. So is it a permanent position? Rachel: No, I'm afraid not. It's a seasonal job, because spring and summer are their busiest time of year. It runs from March until the end of October. But the manager did say that some staff are kept on over the winter, so that might be a possibility. Sam: OK. And what are the hours? Rachel: You'd work four days a week, and they'd like you to start at half past eight in the morning. Sam: That's fine. And what time would I finish? Rachel: Well, the centre stays open until six, but your shift would end at four thirty. Sam: That sounds good. It would give me time to collect my daughter from her after-school club. Rachel: Now, the rate of pay is on the job description, but there are a couple of extra benefits I should mention. All staff get a discount on anything they buy in the centre. Sam: That could be dangerous. I'd probably spend all my wages on plants. Rachel: Well, you'd need to be careful. And the other thing is that if the centre has a good year, staff receive a bonus, which is usually paid just before Christmas. Sam: That's nice. What about lunch? Do staff get meals in the restaurant? Rachel: They don't get free meals, I'm afraid, but there's a staff room with a kitchen where you can make your own lunch. Sam: OK. So what happens next? Rachel: Well, if you're happy for me to do so, I'll send them your CV, and then they'll probably contact you directly to arrange an interview. Sam: Yes, please do that. Thanks very much for thinking of me. Rachel: You're welcome. I'll email you the job description this afternoon. Bye for now. Sam: Bye. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a guide at a heritage site talking to a group of visitors. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Guide: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Millbrook Mill. My name's Chris, and I'm one of the volunteers here. Before you start exploring, I'd like to tell you a little about the history of the site and then explain what you can see in each area. Now, because of the big waterwheel you passed on the way in, most visitors assume that this was a corn mill, where grain was ground into flour. In fact, when it was built in seventeen ninety, the mill was used for spinning cotton, and at its busiest it employed over two hundred people. Later, in the eighteen seventies, it was converted to make paper, and it carried on doing that until it finally closed in nineteen fifty-eight. Guide: You may be wondering about the waterwheel itself. People often ask me whether it's the largest in the country. It isn't, I'm afraid. There are several bigger ones in the north of England. And although there's a story that it was brought here from another mill, that isn't true either. It was made for this building. What makes it special is that it still turns. The river still drives it, and it provides the power for one of the old machines, which we use for demonstrations. Guide: Now, you'll see that the stairs to the second floor are closed off. That floor was rented out as studios for local artists for a few years, and at one time it was used to store the museum's collection. But at the moment, the old wooden floors up there are being repaired, so it isn't safe for visitors. We hope to have it open again by the summer. Guide: One last thing before we move on. If you enjoy your visit, I'd really recommend getting tickets for our evening talk this Friday. It's about the children who worked in the mill, and it's always very popular. Our guidebooks are on sale in the shop as well, but most of the information in them is also on the display boards, so you don't really need one. And if you live locally, you might think about an annual pass, although you can get most of the same benefits by joining our Friends scheme. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Guide: Right, let me tell you about the different areas. The first room you come to is the Counting House, which was the mill office, where the workers' wages were calculated. Most of what you'll see in there, the old ledgers, the clocks and even some of the clothes the mill workers wore, was given to us by families in the village whose grandparents and great-grandparents worked here. It's a lovely collection. Guide: From there, you go into the Wheel Room, where you can see the machinery that connects the waterwheel to the rest of the mill. There's a short film running on a loop in there, which shows how the wheel was restored by volunteers about twenty years ago. It only lasts about ten minutes, and it's well worth watching. Guide: Next is the Dye Shed. This is where the cotton was coloured, using dyes made from plants. We have a demonstration table in there, and visitors are welcome to have a go at dyeing a small piece of cloth, which you can take home with you. Children love it, and they don't need to be with an adult, although it does get a bit messy, so you might want to roll your sleeves up. Guide: After that, you go upstairs to the Weaving Floor. You're free to walk around on your own, you don't need a guide, but when the looms are running it's extremely noisy, so everybody has to put on the ear defenders that you'll find hanging by the door. That applies to adults and children alike. The workers who stood here for twelve hours a day had no such protection, and many of them lost their hearing. Guide: Then there's the Mill Garden, down by the river. Unfortunately, the river flooded last week, and the lower part of the garden is still under water, so we've had to close that section. You can still visit the upper part, though, which has the herb beds and a picnic area. Guide: And finally, there's the Workers' Cottage, just across the yard. It shows how a family of mill workers would have lived in the eighteen hundreds. It was closed for most of last year while the roof was replaced, but it opened again last month, and people are finding it fascinating. It's quite small inside, so we ask you to go in a few at a time. Right, if you'd like to follow me, we'll start in the Counting House. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two trainee teachers, Hannah and Josh, discussing a video of a primary school maths lesson in which children played board games. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 27. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 27. Hannah: So, Josh, the tutor wants us to discuss the video we've just watched and think about whether board games are really a useful way of teaching maths. Josh: Well, I have to say I was surprised. I'd always thought of board games as something you do on a rainy afternoon when the children are tired, not as a proper part of a lesson. Hannah: Me too. But you could see the children were practising some really important skills. What struck me most was how much mental arithmetic they were doing. Every time they moved, they had to add up their score in their heads, and nobody reached for a calculator or even a pencil. Josh: That's right. And I thought it was interesting how they had to wait for their turn. For children of that age, just waiting quietly while someone else takes a long time to decide what to do is a real test of patience. Hannah: Yes, and most of them managed it very well. I was hoping to see a bit more creative thinking, though. They were really just following the instructions on the board. Josh: I suppose that's the nature of a board game. And because they were playing in pairs rather than in bigger groups, there wasn't much chance to see how they'd cope with working in a larger team. Hannah: True. And there wasn't really any reading involved either, apart from the numbers on the cards. Anyway, shall we talk about the individual children? I made some notes on the ones the tutor asked us to look at. Josh: So did I. Let's start with Leo. Hannah: Well, Leo started off really enthusiastically. He was the first to set up the board, and he explained the rules to his partner. But after about ten minutes he was looking out of the window, and by the end he'd stopped paying attention to the game altogether. Josh: Yes, I noticed that. Maybe the game went on for too long for him. What about Maya? Hannah: I thought Maya was lovely. Her partner kept getting his sums wrong, and instead of just telling him the answer, she showed him how to count on using his fingers. By the end he was doing it on his own. Josh: Yes, she was very patient with him. Then there was Oscar. Hannah: Oscar. Well, he certainly knew his numbers. But he got very upset every time his partner moved ahead of him, and at one point he tried to change the score. The teacher had to have a word with him. Josh: Winning seemed to matter far too much to him. I suppose that's one of the risks with games. Priya was interesting, too. Hannah: Yes. She finished her game long before anyone else, and she got every calculation right. She said it was a game for babies, didn't she? Josh: She did. She clearly needs something more challenging, maybe a version with bigger numbers. And finally, Finn. Hannah: Finn hardly said a word at the beginning, and he kept looking at the teacher to check that he was doing the right thing. But once he'd had a couple of turns, he relaxed, and by the end he was laughing with his partner. Josh: Yes, it took him a while to feel comfortable. He's quite a shy boy, I think. He didn't ask for any help, though. Hannah: No, he just watched the others carefully. I expect he'll be much more confident next time. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 28 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 28 to 30. Josh: So, if we used board games in our own classes, what do you think the teacher would need to do before the children start playing? Hannah: Well, some people say you should put children in groups according to their ability, but I don't think that's necessary for a game like this. And I don't think you need to set a strict time limit either. Josh: No. The key thing is that the rules are really clear. The teacher in the video played a round on the whiteboard first, so the children could see exactly what to do. That's why there were so few arguments. Hannah: Absolutely. If the children don't understand the rules, the whole lesson falls apart. Josh: Why do you think more teachers don't use games like this? Is it the cost? Hannah: I don't think so. Most schools already have a cupboard full of old games, and they're cheap to buy anyway. And the teacher in the video managed the noise level quite well. Josh: I think the problem is that some teachers worry that parents and head teachers will see it as just playing, rather than proper learning. They're afraid it will look as though they're wasting time. Hannah: Yes, I think you're right. That's probably the main reason. So, for our teaching practice next term, shall we try using a game in one of our maths lessons? Josh: Good idea. We could buy one of the games that are made for schools. Hannah: They're quite expensive, though. We could ask the children to bring in games from home, but then we wouldn't know what we'd end up with. Josh: What if we got the children to design and make their own game as a class? They'd have to work out the rules and the scoring themselves, and that would involve a lot of maths. Hannah: I love that idea. And they'd probably be much more interested in playing a game they'd made themselves. Let's do that. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a student giving a presentation about a writer and the house where he lived. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: For my presentation, I've chosen to talk about the writer Rudyard Kipling and the house in the south of England where he spent the second half of his life. Most people know Kipling's name, and many of you will have seen the Disney film of The Jungle Book. But I think far fewer people know much about the man himself, or about the house, which is now open to the public. Student: Kipling was born in India in eighteen sixty-five. When he was five, his parents sent him to England to be educated, which was quite common for British families in India at that time, and he was very unhappy there. He went back to India at the age of sixteen and worked as a journalist on a newspaper in Lahore. He wrote articles and short stories, and it was through these that he first became known as a writer. Today, he's probably best known for the stories he wrote for children, such as The Jungle Book and the Just So Stories. But he also wrote poems, novels and a great many stories for adults, and in nineteen oh seven he became the first English-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. His reputation has changed a great deal since then. In his lifetime he was enormously popular, but later some of his views about the British Empire made him a controversial figure, and critics still disagree about how he should be judged. Student: Kipling married an American woman, Carrie Balestier, and the couple went to live in her home country. It was while they were living in Vermont that he wrote The Jungle Book. The house they built there still stands today. However, after a bitter quarrel with Carrie's brother, they returned to England. They settled in the village of Rottingdean, on the south coast, which is now really part of the city of Brighton, but by then Kipling was so famous that tourists used to come and stand outside the house hoping to see him. What he wanted more than anything was privacy, and so the family began looking for somewhere more isolated. Student: Kipling was one of the first people in England to own a car, and he loved exploring the countryside. It was by car that he and Carrie first came across Bateman's, a stone house in a quiet valley in East Sussex. They are said to have fallen in love with it the moment they saw it, and they bought it in nineteen oh two, and Kipling lived there for the rest of his life. Student: The house was built in the sixteen thirties for a man who had made his fortune from the local iron industry, which was important in that part of England at the time. Kipling loved the fact that it was so old. There was a watermill on the property, and Kipling, who was very interested in new technology, had a turbine installed in the mill so that it could generate electricity for the house. It was only enough to light a few bulbs for a couple of hours each evening, but it was quite unusual at that time. Student: If you visit the house today, the room most people want to see is Kipling's study, on the first floor. It's been kept exactly as he left it. The walls are lined with books, and his desk is still covered with the objects he liked to have around him while he was writing. He used to say that he couldn't write unless everything was in its proper place. The countryside around the house, and its long history, also inspired some of his later work, including Puck of Pook's Hill, a collection of stories about the history of England. Student: However, the years at Bateman's were not all happy. Kipling's only son, John, was killed in the First World War, in nineteen fifteen, when he was just eighteen. His body was not identified until many years later. After the war, Kipling worked for the War Graves Commission, which was responsible for the cemeteries and memorials to soldiers who had died. He chose many of the words that appear on the gravestones and memorials, which you can still see today. Student: Kipling died in nineteen thirty-six. His wife continued to live at Bateman's, and when she died, three years later, she left the house to the National Trust, which has looked after it ever since. Many of the rooms are furnished as they were when the Kiplings lived there, and the gardens and the mill are also open to visitors. I'd really recommend a visit, if you're ever in that part of the country. I visited it myself last summer, and I've included some of my photographs on the next few slides. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

Thanks very much for thinking of me. Rachel: You're welcome. I'll email you the job description this afternoon. Bye for now. Sam: Bye. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a guide at a heritage site talking to a group of visitors. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Guide: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Millbrook Mill. My name's Chris, and I'm one of the volunteers here. Before you start exploring, I'd like to tell you a little about the history of the site and then explain what you can see in each area. Now, because of the big waterwheel you passed on the way in, most visitors assume that this was a corn mill, where grain was ground into flour. In fact, when it was built in seventeen ninety, the mill was used for spinning cotton, and at its busiest it employed over two hundred people. Later, in the eighteen seventies, it was converted to make paper, and it carried on doing that until it finally closed in nineteen fifty-eight. Guide: You may be wondering about the waterwheel itself. People often ask me whether it's the largest in the country. It isn't, I'm afraid. There are several bigger ones in the north of England. And although there's a story that it was brought here from another mill, that isn't true either. It was made for this building. What makes it special is that it still turns. The river still drives it, and it provides the power for one of the old machines, which we use for demonstrations. Guide: Now, you'll see that the stairs to the second floor are closed off. That floor was rented out as studios for local artists for a few years, and at one time it was used to store the museum's collection. But at the moment, the old wooden floors up there are being repaired, so it isn't safe for visitors. We hope to have it open again by the summer. Guide: One last thing before we move on. If you enjoy your visit, I'd really recommend getting tickets for our evening talk this Friday. It's about the children who worked in the mill, and it's always very popular. Our guidebooks are on sale in the shop as well, but most of the information in them is also on the display boards, so you don't really need one. And if you live locally, you might think about an annual pass, although you can get most of the same benefits by joining our Friends scheme. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Guide: Right, let me tell you about the different areas. The first room you come to is the Counting House, which was the mill office, where the workers' wages were calculated. Most of what you'll see in there, the old ledgers, the clocks and even some of the clothes the mill workers wore, was given to us by families in the village whose grandparents and great-grandparents worked here. It's a lovely collection. Guide: From there, you go into the Wheel Room, where you can see the machinery that connects the waterwheel to the rest of the mill. There's a short film running on a loop in there, which shows how the wheel was restored by volunteers about twenty years ago. It only lasts about ten minutes, and it's well worth watching. Guide: Next is the Dye Shed. This is where the cotton was coloured, using dyes made from plants. We have a demonstration table in there, and visitors are welcome to have a go at dyeing a small piece of cloth, which you can take home with you. Children love it, and they don't need to be with an adult, although it does get a bit messy, so you might want to roll your sleeves up. Guide: After that, you go upstairs to the Weaving Floor. You're free to walk around on your own, you don't need a guide, but when the looms are running it's extremely noisy, so everybody has to put on the ear defenders that you'll find hanging by the door. That applies to adults and children alike. The workers who stood here for twelve hours a day had no such protection, and many of them lost their hearing. Guide: Then there's the Mill Garden, down by the river. Unfortunately, the river flooded last week, and the lower part of the garden is still under water, so we've had to close that section. You can still visit the upper part, though, which has the herb beds and a picnic area. Guide: And finally, there's the Workers' Cottage, just across the yard. It shows how a family of mill workers would have lived in the eighteen hundreds. It was closed for most of last year while the roof was replaced, but it opened again last month, and people are finding it fascinating. It's quite small inside, so we ask you to go in a few at a time. Right, if you'd like to follow me, we'll start in the Counting House. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two trainee teachers, Hannah and Josh, discussing a video of a primary school maths lesson in which children played board games. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 27. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 27. Hannah: So, Josh, the tutor wants us to discuss the video we've just watched and think about whether board games are really a useful way of teaching maths. Josh: Well, I have to say I was surprised. I'd always thought of board games as something you do on a rainy afternoon when the children are tired, not as a proper part of a lesson. Hannah: Me too. But you could see the children were practising some really important skills. What struck me most was how much mental arithmetic they were doing. Every time they moved, they had to add up their score in their heads, and nobody reached for a calculator or even a pencil. Josh: That's right. And I thought it was interesting how they had to wait for their turn. For children of that age, just waiting quietly while someone else takes a long time to decide what to do is a real test of patience. Hannah: Yes, and most of them managed it very well. I was hoping to see a bit more creative thinking, though. They were really just following the instructions on the board. Josh: I suppose that's the nature of a board game. And because they were playing in pairs rather than in bigger groups, there wasn't much chance to see how they'd cope with working in a larger team. Hannah: True. And there wasn't really any reading involved either, apart from the numbers on the cards. Anyway, shall we talk about the individual children? I made some notes on the ones the tutor asked us to look at. Josh: So did I. Let's start with Leo. Hannah: Well, Leo started off really enthusiastically. He was the first to set up the board, and he explained the rules to his partner. But after about ten minutes he was looking out of the window, and by the end he'd stopped paying attention to the game altogether. Josh: Yes, I noticed that. Maybe the game went on for too long for him. What about Maya? Hannah: I thought Maya was lovely. Her partner kept getting his sums wrong, and instead of just telling him the answer, she showed him how to count on using his fingers. By the end he was doing it on his own. Josh: Yes, she was very patient with him. Then there was Oscar. Hannah: Oscar. Well, he certainly knew his numbers. But he got very upset every time his partner moved ahead of him, and at one point he tried to change the score. The teacher had to have a word with him. Josh: Winning seemed to matter far too much to him. I suppose that's one of the risks with games. Priya was interesting, too. Hannah: Yes. She finished her game long before anyone else, and she got every calculation right. She said it was a game for babies, didn't she? Josh: She did. She clearly needs something more challenging, maybe a version with bigger numbers. And finally, Finn. Hannah: Finn hardly said a word at the beginning, and he kept looking at the teacher to check that he was doing the right thing. But once he'd had a couple of turns, he relaxed, and by the end he was laughing with his partner. Josh: Yes, it took him a while to feel comfortable. He's quite a shy boy, I think. He didn't ask for any help, though. Hannah: No, he just watched the others carefully. I expect he'll be much more confident next time. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 28 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 28 to 30. Josh: So, if we used board games in our own classes, what do you think the teacher would need to do before the children start playing? Hannah: Well, some people say you should put children in groups according to their ability, but I don't think that's necessary for a game like this. And I don't think you need to set a strict time limit either. Josh: No. The key thing is that the rules are really clear. The teacher in the video played a round on the whiteboard first, so the children could see exactly what to do. That's why there were so few arguments. Hannah: Absolutely. If the children don't understand the rules, the whole lesson falls apart. Josh: Why do you think more teachers don't use games like this? Is it the cost? Hannah: I don't think so. Most schools already have a cupboard full of old games, and they're cheap to buy anyway. And the teacher in the video managed the noise level quite well. Josh: I think the problem is that some teachers worry that parents and head teachers will see it as just playing, rather than proper learning. They're afraid it will look as though they're wasting time. Hannah: Yes, I think you're right. That's probably the main reason. So, for our teaching practice next term, shall we try using a game in one of our maths lessons? Josh: Good idea. We could buy one of the games that are made for schools. Hannah: They're quite expensive, though. We could ask the children to bring in games from home, but then we wouldn't know what we'd end up with. Josh: What if we got the children to design and make their own game as a class? They'd have to work out the rules and the scoring themselves, and that would involve a lot of maths. Hannah: I love that idea. And they'd probably be much more interested in playing a game they'd made themselves. Let's do that. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a student giving a presentation about a writer and the house where he lived. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Student: For my presentation, I've chosen to talk about the writer Rudyard Kipling and the house in the south of England where he spent the second half of his life. Most people know Kipling's name, and many of you will have seen the Disney film of The Jungle Book. But I think far fewer people know much about the man himself, or about the house, which is now open to the public. Student: Kipling was born in India in eighteen sixty-five. When he was five, his parents sent him to England to be educated, which was quite common for British families in India at that time, and he was very unhappy there. He went back to India at the age of sixteen and worked as a journalist on a newspaper in Lahore. He wrote articles and short stories, and it was through these that he first became known as a writer. Today, he's probably best known for the stories he wrote for children, such as The Jungle Book and the Just So Stories. But he also wrote poems, novels and a great many stories for adults, and in nineteen oh seven he became the first English-language writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. His reputation has changed a great deal since then. In his lifetime he was enormously popular, but later some of his views about the British Empire made him a controversial figure, and critics still disagree about how he should be judged. Student: Kipling married an American woman, Carrie Balestier, and the couple went to live in her home country. It was while they were living in Vermont that he wrote The Jungle Book. The house they built there still stands today. However, after a bitter quarrel with Carrie's brother, they returned to England. They settled in the village of Rottingdean, on the south coast, which is now really part of the city of Brighton, but by then Kipling was so famous that tourists used to come and stand outside the house hoping to see him. What he wanted more than anything was privacy, and so the family began looking for somewhere more isolated. Student: Kipling was one of the first people in England to own a car, and he loved exploring the countryside. It was by car that he and Carrie first came across Bateman's, a stone house in a quiet valley in East Sussex. They are said to have fallen in love with it the moment they saw it, and they bought it in nineteen oh two, and Kipling lived there for the rest of his life. Student: The house was built in the sixteen thirties for a man who had made his fortune from the local iron industry, which was important in that part of England at the time. Kipling loved the fact that it was so old. There was a watermill on the property, and Kipling, who was very interested in new technology, had a turbine installed in the mill so that it could generate electricity for the house. It was only enough to light a few bulbs for a couple of hours each evening, but it was quite unusual at that time. Student: If you visit the house today, the room most people want to see is Kipling's study, on the first floor. It's been kept exactly as he left it. The walls are lined with books, and his desk is still covered with the objects he liked to have around him while he was writing. He used to say that he couldn't write unless everything was in its proper place. The countryside around the house, and its long history, also inspired some of his later work, including Puck of Pook's Hill, a collection of stories about the history of England. Student: However, the years at Bateman's were not all happy. Kipling's only son, John, was killed in the First World War, in nineteen fifteen, when he was just eighteen. His body was not identified until many years later. After the war, Kipling worked for the War Graves Commission, which was responsible for the cemeteries and memorials to soldiers who had died. He chose many of the words that appear on the gravestones and memorials, which you can still see today. Student: Kipling died in nineteen thirty-six. His wife continued to live at Bateman's, and when she died, three years later, she left the house to the National Trust, which has looked after it ever since. Many of the rooms are furnished as they were when the Kiplings lived there, and the gardens and the mill are also open to visitors. I'd really recommend a visit, if you're ever in that part of the country. I visited it myself last summer, and I've included some of my photographs on the next few slides. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
